passages.t: Ziba's gifts, and a charge against his master
passages.happening:
Just past the summit Ziba, the servant of Mephibosheth, meets David with two saddled donkeys loaded with bread, raisins, summer fruit and a skin of wine: donkeys for the king's household, food for the young men, wine for anyone who grows faint in the wilderness (verses 1-2).

“Where is your master’s grandson?” asked the king (verse 3). Ziba answers that Mephibosheth has stayed in Jerusalem, hoping that Israel will now give him back his grandfather Saul's kingdom.

So the king said to Ziba, “All that belongs to Mephibosheth is now yours!” (verse 4). Ziba bows and thanks him.
passages.hearers:
The chapter moves back and forth between the fleeing king and the new king in the capital. On the road David meets two men from Saul's world, one bringing gifts and one bringing curses, and both test his judgment.

Ziba's gifts are real and welcome, and they come with a story. David has only Ziba's word for what Mephibosheth said, and he decides at once, giving away all that he had restored to Jonathan's son (chapter 9). Whether Ziba told the truth is a question the book leaves open until chapter 19, when Mephibosheth gives his own account.
passages.later: A proverb warns against a judgment made on one side of a story: “The first to state his case seems right until another comes and cross-examines him” (Proverbs 18:17).
passages.asks: David judged Mephibosheth on one man's word, at a moment when he was frightened and grateful. Ask how you avoid making decisions on one side of a story. And ask whom you might have judged too quickly in a hard week.

passages.happening:
As David comes near Bahurim, a man from Saul's family, Shimei son of Gera, comes out cursing and throwing stones at David and his servants. “Get out, get out, you worthless man of bloodshed! The LORD has paid you back for all the blood of the house of Saul, in whose place you have reigned, and the LORD has delivered the kingdom into the hand of your son Absalom. See, you have come to ruin because you are a man of bloodshed!” (verses 7-8).

Abishai asks leave to go over and cut off his head. David refuses. His own son seeks his life, he says, so how much more this Benjamite. ‘Leave him alone and let him curse me, for the LORD has told him so. Perhaps the LORD will see my affliction and repay me with good for the cursing I receive today’ (verses 11-12).

So David and his men go on along the road, while Shimei walks along the hillside opposite, cursing and throwing stones and dust. The king and all the people arrive exhausted, and there he rests (verses 13-14).
passages.hearers:
Bahurim was a village in Benjamin, just east of Jerusalem on the road down to the Jordan. Shimei belonged to Saul's clan, and his curses show that the house of Saul still had people who saw David as a usurper.

His charge that David shed the blood of Saul's house may point to the deaths of Abner and Ish-bosheth, which David had publicly disowned, or to the seven descendants of Saul in chapter 21, if that came earlier. Either way it shows how David's rise looked to Saul's family. And it lands where Shimei may not have meant it to. David did not kill Saul or his heirs, but he did shed Uriah's blood, and the reader knows it.

A curse was a spoken wish for harm, often calling on God, and it was taken seriously. Throwing stones and dust was insult and threat at once. Abishai calls Shimei a dead dog, the very words Mephibosheth once used of himself. David's answer, ‘What have I to do with you, O sons of Zeruiah’ (verse 10), is a sharp way of putting distance between himself and his nephews' violence.

David's response is the center of the chapter. He will not answer violence with violence. He reads the curse as something God may have allowed or even sent, and he hopes that God will see his trouble and repay it with good.
passages.later:
Psalm 3, headed for this flight, speaks of the many who say that God will not deliver him (Psalm 3:2), almost what Shimei shouted.

David did not forget the curses. Near his death he told Solomon, ‘Keep an eye on Shimei the son of Gera, the Benjamite from Bahurim’ (1 Kings 2:8).
passages.hard:
Did God really tell Shimei to curse David?

David says, ‘the LORD has told him so’ (verse 11), and interpreters read his words in different ways. Some take them as David's humble recognition that God rules all things, even the malice of others, so that an enemy's curses can be used by God to discipline him, without making God the author of Shimei's sin. Others take them as a statement of David's uncertainty, since the verse before begins with if, and of his resolve to leave judgment to God rather than act on his own.

In either case, David does not approve of what Shimei does, and he later asks Solomon to deal with him. The chapter does not teach that every curse comes from God. It shows David, humbled by his own sin, choosing to bear this one rather than add to the bloodshed.
passages.asks: David chose not to strike back at a man who cursed him. Ask when you have been tempted to answer an insult with force. And ask whether there is any truth in a hard word spoken against you that you need to hear, even from someone who meant you harm.

passages.t: Hushai, Ahithophel, and the roof of the palace
passages.happening:
Absalom comes into Jerusalem with all the men of Israel, and Ahithophel with him. David's friend Hushai goes to Absalom: “Long live the king! Long live the king!” (verse 16). Absalom asks why he did not go with his friend. Hushai answers that he will serve the one chosen by the LORD and the people, and that as he served the father, he will serve the son (verses 18-19).

Absalom asks Ahithophel for counsel. Ahithophel answers, “Sleep with your father’s concubines, whom he has left to keep the palace. When all Israel hears that you have become a stench to your father, then the hands of all who are with you will be strengthened” (verse 21).

‘So they pitched a tent for Absalom on the roof, and he slept with his father’s concubines in the sight of all Israel’ (verse 22). In those days Ahithophel's advice was regarded ‘like the consultation of the word of God’ (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Hushai's words have a double meaning. Long live the king, he says, without saying which king, and he promises to serve the one the LORD has chosen, without saying who that is. Absalom hears what he wants to hear.

Ahithophel's counsel is cold political calculation. Taking a king's concubines was a public claim to his throne, and Ahithophel means the act to make any reconciliation between father and son impossible, so that Absalom's followers need not fear being abandoned in a bargain between them. That is what he means by becoming a stench to his father.

The ten women had been left to keep the palace (15:16). Now they are violated in a tent on the palace roof, in front of all Israel, used as a sign of one man's power over another. The text gives them no voice at all. Nathan had said that this would happen: another man would lie with David's wives in broad daylight (12:11-12). It happens on the same roof from which David first saw Bathsheba. The judgment falls on David, but it is the women who bear it.

The chapter's last note explains why David so feared Ahithophel's going over to Absalom. His counsel was held in extraordinary regard, and the next chapter will turn on it.
passages.later: The same claim was made long before, when Jacob's eldest son ‘went in and slept with his father’s concubine Bilhah’ (Genesis 35:22), and Solomon later heard a request for his father's companion Abishag as a bid for the throne (1 Kings 2:22).
passages.hard:
Absalom takes his father's concubines on the roof. How should a reader see these women?

The text tells the act in one sentence and gives no word from them. Nothing in the text suggests that they could refuse the man who now held the palace, and they were used as a public sign of his claim. That is sexual violence and the abuse of power, whatever the politics around it. The narrator records it as the fulfillment of Nathan's word against David, and the women are not to blame for any of it. When David returns, he will provide for them but shut them away for the rest of their lives (20:3), and they are never heard from.

A word for anyone who has been sexually assaulted. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. Where you were, what you wore, whether you fought back: none of it makes it your fault. Please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Absalom chose an act that would burn every bridge behind him. Ask what actions in your own relationships make reconciliation impossible. And ask who pays when powerful people use others to make a point.
